content: Acute liver failure is a rare and life-threatening condition that can be caused by paracetamol (acetaminophen) or other factors unrelated to paracetamol. Non-paracetamol-related acute liver failure has a particularly poor prognosis and limited treatment options. N-acetylcysteine has been shown to be effective in treating paracetamol-induced acute liver failure, reducing the need for liver transplantation. Recent randomized clinical trials have investigated whether this benefit extends to cases of acute liver failure not caused by paracetamol. The 2011 guidelines from the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) suggested that N-acetylcysteine might improve survival in patients with non-paracetamol-related acute liver failure if administered during the early stages of encephalopathy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of N-acetylcysteine compared to placebo or no N-acetylcysteine, in addition to standard care, for patients with non-paracetamol-related acute liver failure. The review included randomized clinical trials that compared any dose or route of N-acetylcysteine with placebo or no intervention in this patient population. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used, including meta-analyses, risk ratio calculations, and assessments of bias and evidence certainty using the GRADE approach. Two randomized clinical trials were included in the review. One trial involved 183 adults, and the other included 174 children (from birth to 17 years of age). Both trials were assessed as having a high overall risk of bias. An additional unregistered study in adults is awaiting classification, pending further information from the study authors regarding trial methodology, such as randomization processes. The evidence for all-cause mortality at 21 days in adults treated with N-acetylcysteine compared to placebo was inconclusive. In the adult trial, 29.6% of participants receiving N-acetylcysteine died, compared to 33.7% in the placebo group (risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57 to 1.37). The certainty of this evidence was rated as low due to bias and imprecision. Similarly, for all-cause mortality at one year in children, the evidence was also inconclusive. In the pediatric trial, 27.2% of children receiving N-acetylcysteine died, compared to 18.5% in the placebo group (RR 1.47, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.53). The certainty of this evidence was downgraded to very low due to serious imprecision. The review did not perform meta-analyses for serious adverse events or liver transplantation rates at one year due to incomplete reporting and clinical heterogeneity. For liver transplantation at 21 days in adults, the evidence was inconclusive (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.06), with low certainty due to bias and imprecision. Similarly, for liver transplantation at one year in children, the evidence was also inconclusive (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.81), with very low certainty due to serious imprecision. The evidence for serious adverse events in children was inconclusive (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.35 to 4.51), with very low certainty due to serious imprecision. Non-serious adverse events were not meta-analyzed due to clinical heterogeneity. In adults, the evidence for non-serious adverse events was inconclusive (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.45; 173 participants), with low certainty. Similarly, in children, the evidence for non-serious adverse events was also inconclusive (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.16; 184 participants), with low certainty. None of the trials reported outcomes related to the resolution of encephalopathy or coagulopathy, nor did they assess health-related quality of life. Both trials were funded by grants from the National Institutes of Health in the United States, with additional funding from hospital foundations for one trial. Pharmaceutical companies provided the study drug and matching placebo but did not influence the study design or analysis. In conclusion, the available evidence is insufficient to determine whether N-acetylcysteine is beneficial compared to placebo or no N-acetylcysteine for patients with non-paracetamol-related acute liver failure. The current evidence does not support the guideline recommendation to use N-acetylcysteine in adults with this condition, nor does it justify the increasing use of N-acetylcysteine in clinical practice. Further randomized clinical trials are needed to evaluate the efficacy of N-acetylcysteine in this context, as well as to identify predictors of response and determine the optimal dose and duration of treatment.
